_Colby Grimes, Colby Chamber, Jonathan Graves, Manas Mridul, Valeria Zolla_ date: 9 July 2023 description: An introduction to analyzing data using tidyverse and dplyr in R including workflows for loading, merging, cleaning and visualizing data. categories: [introduction, getting started, R, data, tidyverse, data cleaning, tables, data wrangling, missing values, merging data] execute: eval: true echo: true output: true format: html: default ipynb: jupyter: kernelspec: display_name: R language: r name: ir image: /media/comet_placeholder.png --- ## Outline ### Prerequisites - Introduction to Data in R - Part 1 ### Learning Outcomes In this notebook, you will learn about: - Filtering, segmenting, combining and cleaning datasets with `tidyverse` and base R - Reshaping and presenting data in different kinds of formats ### References - [Introduction to Probability and Statistics Using R](https://mran.microsoft.com/snapshot/2018-09-28/web/packages/IPSUR/vignettes/IPSUR.pdf) - [DSCI 100 Textbook](https://datasciencebook.ca/index.html) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # run this cell source("getting_started_intro_to_data_tests_2.r") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Warning: package 'digest' was built under R version 4.4.2 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Warning: package 'tidyverse' was built under R version 4.4.3 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Warning: package 'ggplot2' was built under R version 4.4.3 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Warning: package 'tibble' was built under R version 4.4.2 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Warning: package 'tidyr' was built under R version 4.4.2 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Warning: package 'readr' was built under R version 4.4.2 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Warning: package 'purrr' was built under R version 4.4.3 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Warning: package 'dplyr' was built under R version 4.4.3 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Warning: package 'stringr' was built under R version 4.4.2 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Warning: package 'forcats' was built under R version 4.4.2 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Warning: package 'lubridate' was built under R version 4.4.2 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Warning: package 'haven' was built under R version 4.4.2 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # loading in our packages library(tidyverse) library(haven) ``` ::: ## Part 1: Data Cleaning The World Development Indicators (WDI) is the primary World Bank collection of development indicators, compiled from officially recognized international sources. We have used the World Bank's DataBank applet to select and import some macro and development-related time series data for the countries Canada, India, Mexico, South Africa, and Zimbabwe for years 2014-2022. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # importing required packages library(readr) library(dplyr) library(tidyr) library(stringr) #Loading the CSV file using the URL file_path <- "datasets/WDI_raw.csv" wdi <- read_csv(file_path) %>% rename(Series_Code = "Series Code", Series_Name = "Series Name", Country = "Country Name", Country_Code = "Country Code") head(wdi, 10) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 10 × 9 Country Country_Code Series_Name Series_Code `2018 [YR2018]` `2019 [YR2019]` 1 India IND School enro… SE.PRM.ENRR 97.4 96.8 2 India IND Access to c… EG.CFT.ACC… 59.5 63.3 3 India IND Access to c… EG.CFT.ACC… 40.9 46.2 4 India IND Access to c… EG.CFT.ACC… 89.1 90.6 5 India IND Access to e… EG.ELC.ACC… 95.7 95.9 6 India IND Access to e… EG.ELC.ACC… 93.9 93.8 7 India IND Access to e… EG.ELC.ACC… 99.1 99.8 8 India IND Account own… FX.OWN.TOT… NA NA 9 India IND Account own… FX.OWN.TOT… NA NA 10 India IND Account own… FX.OWN.TOT… NA NA # ℹ 3 more variables: `2020 [YR2020]` , `2021 [YR2021]` , # `2022 [YR2022]` ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dim(wdi) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 299 9 ``` ::: ::: The data frame is in long format. Each unique value in `Series_Name` is an entry for a row, and not a column. As an example: | Country | Year | Var | Value | |-----:|-----:|-----:|-----:| | Canada | 2017 | Var A | Value | | Canada | 2017 | Var B | Value | | Canada | 2018 | Var C | Value | | Canada | 2018 | Var B | Value | | Canada | 2018 | Var C | Value | A simpler version of the data frame in a **wide-format** could look like this: | Country | Year | Var A | Var B | Var C | |-----:|-----:|-----:|-----:|-----:| | Canada | 2017 | Value | Value | Value | | Canada | 2018 | Value | Value | Value | > **Note**: look up the functions `pivot_wider()` and `pivot_longer()` to learn how to switch between long and wide formats. While `Series_Name` contains descriptions for each of the series in the data frame, `Series_Code` offers a handy way to group variables. Our `Series_Code` variable follows a taxonomy system. For example, any code starting with `AG` belongs to a *family of series* related to the state of agriculture in that country. Let's see the unique series families and their sub series names. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} Series_Families <- wdi %>% mutate(Series_Family = substr(`Series_Code`, 1, 2)) %>% # substring first two characters group_by(Series_Family) %>% # group by unique vals summarize(Series_Names_Under_Family = paste(unique(`Series_Name`), collapse = ", ")) # for each family, find and paste all `Series_Name` head(Series_Families, 13) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 9 × 2 Series_Family Series_Names_Under_Family 1 AG Agricultural land (sq. km), Agricultural machinery, tractors 2 BN Current account balance (BoP, current US$) 3 EG Access to clean fuels and technologies for cooking (% of popula… 4 FX Account ownership at a financial institution or with a mobile-m… 5 IQ CPIA debt policy rating (1=low to 6=high), CPIA macroeconomic m… 6 NV Agriculture, forestry, and fishing, value added (constant 2015 … 7 NY Adjusted net national income per capita (current US$) 8 SE School enrollment, primary (% gross), Adjusted net enrollment r… 9 NA ``` ::: ::: Let's create a data frame with series families related to access to institutions. Those are grouped under `SE` (Schooling), `FX` (Financial Institutions) and `EG` (Electricity). Let's call our dataset `access_wdi`. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} prefixes <- c("SE", "EG", "FX") access_wdi <- wdi %>% filter(str_detect(`Series_Code`, str_c("^", prefixes, collapse = "|"))) access_wdi <- access_wdi %>% rename_with(~str_extract(., "\\d{4}"), starts_with("20")) # rename year columns to follow the 2XYZ format. head(access_wdi, 5) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 5 × 9 Country Country_Code Series_Name Series_Code `2018` `2019` `2020` `2021` 1 India IND School enrollmen… SE.PRM.ENRR 97.4 96.8 99.9 102. 2 India IND Access to clean … EG.CFT.ACC… 59.5 63.3 67.3 71.1 3 India IND Access to clean … EG.CFT.ACC… 40.9 46.2 51.4 56.9 4 India IND Access to clean … EG.CFT.ACC… 89.1 90.6 92 93.3 5 India IND Access to electr… EG.ELC.ACC… 95.7 95.9 96.5 99.6 # ℹ 1 more variable: `2022` ``` ::: ::: ### Handling missing values We are interested in seeing if there are any specific years for when the data was not collected or is missing for *most* of the variables/series. Let's look at each of the year columns and count the number of rows with `NA`. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} year_columns <- c("2018", "2019", "2020", "2021", "2022") missing_counts <- sapply(year_columns, function(column) sum(is.na(access_wdi[[column]]))) # create custom function to count missing values print(missing_counts / nrow(access_wdi)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 2018 2019 2020 2021 2022 0.4505495 0.4835165 0.4890110 0.3186813 0.9835165 ``` ::: ::: Looks like 98% of the data is missing for the year 2022. It probably makes sense to drop the 2022 column altogether. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} access_wdi <- access_wdi %>% select(-`2022`) head(access_wdi, 20) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 20 × 8 Country Country_Code Series_Name Series_Code `2018` `2019` `2020` `2021` 1 India IND School enrollme… SE.PRM.ENRR 97.4 96.8 99.9 102. 2 India IND Access to clean… EG.CFT.ACC… 59.5 63.3 67.3 71.1 3 India IND Access to clean… EG.CFT.ACC… 40.9 46.2 51.4 56.9 4 India IND Access to clean… EG.CFT.ACC… 89.1 90.6 92 93.3 5 India IND Access to elect… EG.ELC.ACC… 95.7 95.9 96.5 99.6 6 India IND Access to elect… EG.ELC.ACC… 93.9 93.8 95.2 99.3 7 India IND Access to elect… EG.ELC.ACC… 99.1 99.8 99 100 8 India IND Account ownersh… FX.OWN.TOT… NA NA NA 77.5 9 India IND Account ownersh… FX.OWN.TOT… NA NA NA 77.6 10 India IND Account ownersh… FX.OWN.TOT… NA NA NA 77.5 11 India IND Adjusted net en… SE.PRM.TEN… NA NA NA NA 12 India IND Adjusted net en… SE.PRM.TEN… NA NA NA NA 13 India IND Adjusted net en… SE.PRM.TENR NA NA NA NA 14 Canada CAN School enrollme… SE.PRM.ENRR 102. 101. 102. NA 15 Canada CAN Access to clean… EG.CFT.ACC… 100 100 100 100 16 Canada CAN Access to clean… EG.CFT.ACC… 100 100 100 100 17 Canada CAN Access to clean… EG.CFT.ACC… 100 100 100 100 18 Canada CAN Access to elect… EG.ELC.ACC… 100 100 100 100 19 Canada CAN Access to elect… EG.ELC.ACC… 100 100 100 100 20 Canada CAN Access to elect… EG.ELC.ACC… 100 100 100 100 ``` ::: ::: Now let's check for missing values *row-wise* - whether there are lots of NAs for a country-series combination. Let's check if there are any particular country-series combination for which the data is missing for more than 2 years. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # create new column with NA count by columns for each row access_wdi$count_na <- rowSums(is.na(access_wdi)) # sort by number of missing vals access_wdi <- access_wdi %>% arrange(desc(count_na)) select(access_wdi, c("Country_Code", "Series_Code", "count_na")) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 182 × 3 Country_Code Series_Code count_na 1 IND SE.PRM.TENR.MA 4 2 IND SE.PRM.TENR.FE 4 3 IND SE.PRM.TENR 4 4 CAN SE.PRM.TENR.MA 4 5 CAN SE.PRM.TENR.FE 4 6 CAN SE.PRM.TENR 4 7 HND SE.PRM.ENRR 4 8 HND SE.PRM.TENR.MA 4 9 HND SE.PRM.TENR.FE 4 10 HND SE.PRM.TENR 4 # ℹ 172 more rows ``` ::: ::: This data frame shows that we don't have *any* data for series beginning with the `SE` (Schooling) prefix. > **Think Deeper**: how could you be systematic when choosing whether to drop or not NA values? Our panel dataset is indexed by country and series, and we're interested in yearly values over time. Think about the options we have to drop NAs: (1) Dropping a series altogether (2) Dropping specific countries (3) Dropping specific rows (i.e., country-series pairs)... Let's create an array with `Series_Code` to be dropped from our dataset. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # creating an array of `Series_Code` that need to be dropped from access_wdi to_drop <- access_wdi %>% filter(count_na > 2) %>% distinct(Series_Code) %>% unique() to_drop <- unlist(to_drop, use.names = FALSE) to_drop ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "SE.PRM.TENR.MA" "SE.PRM.TENR.FE" "SE.PRM.TENR" [4] "SE.PRM.ENRR" "FX.OWN.TOTL.ZS" "FX.OWN.TOTL.FE.ZS" [7] "FX.OWN.TOTL.MA.ZS" "EG.CFT.ACCS.ZS" "EG.CFT.ACCS.RU.ZS" [10] "EG.CFT.ACCS.UR.ZS" ``` ::: ::: > **Think Deeper**: what if dropping the missing values leads to low sample size issues? One approach is to import data from alternative sources and *fill them into* our original data set. This topic is beyond the scope of this notebook, but think about the implications of filling in data to the study. Let's now drop all the rows where `Series_Code` matches any of the codes in `to_drop`, and save the resulting data frame as a new version of `access_wdi`. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} filtered_access_wdi <- access_wdi %>% filter(!(Series_Code %in% to_drop)) filtered_access_wdi ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 42 × 9 Country Country_Code Series_Name Series_Code `2018` `2019` `2020` `2021` 1 India IND Access to ele… EG.ELC.ACC… 95.7 95.9 96.5 99.6 2 India IND Access to ele… EG.ELC.ACC… 93.9 93.8 95.2 99.3 3 India IND Access to ele… EG.ELC.ACC… 99.1 99.8 99 100 4 Canada CAN Access to ele… EG.ELC.ACC… 100 100 100 100 5 Canada CAN Access to ele… EG.ELC.ACC… 100 100 100 100 6 Canada CAN Access to ele… EG.ELC.ACC… 100 100 100 100 7 Honduras HND Access to ele… EG.ELC.ACC… 91.6 91.1 93.1 94.1 8 Honduras HND Access to ele… EG.ELC.ACC… 81.9 80.3 83.4 85.7 9 Honduras HND Access to ele… EG.ELC.ACC… 98.9 99 100 100 10 Indonesia IDN Access to ele… EG.ELC.ACC… 98.5 98.8 97.0 99.2 # ℹ 32 more rows # ℹ 1 more variable: count_na ``` ::: ::: Now the only variables left in this data frame are the `EG` variables, which indicate the levels of access to electricity and other power sources within the countries. This dataset is clearly not appropriate to answer questions about overall access to institutions; however, it could be extremely useful if the scope of the research is narrowed to access to power utilities. For example, we could use the dataset to visualize the growth in access to energy across the countries over the last 5 years. ### Test your knowledge Before you complete the following exercises, take a moment to review the section above. Are there any functions you're not familiar with? Now is a good time to learn them. > **Note**: by running `?function_name` you can get a detailed description of any of the functions used in this notebook. What are some possible ways to deal with NA values? Select all that apply (A) Drop them row-wise (B) Drop them column-wise (C) Fill them in (D) Change the scope of the research ::: {.cell .question} ```{.r .cell-code} # Enter your answer as a string (in alphabetical order) with your answer choices ex: "ACD" answer_1 <- test_1() ``` ::: ::: {.cell .answer} ```{.r .cell-code} answer_1 <- "ABCD" test_1() ``` ::: What is normally the best way to deal with missing data? (A) Drop them row-wise (B) Drop them column-wise (C) Fill them in (D) Change the scope of the research (E) Impossible to tell ::: {.cell .question} ```{.r .cell-code} # Enter your answer as either "A", "B", "C", "D", or "E" answer_2 <- test_2() ``` ::: ::: {.cell .answer} ```{.r .cell-code} answer_2 <- "E" test_2() ``` ::: ## Part 2: Merging data frames in R Now let's take a step back and consider an example of merging data frames. Our WDI data set has macro information on *national incomes*, *CABs*, *Bank Capital to Assets Ratios,* and various kinds of *CPIA* ratings. Let's extract that data and merge it with data from the Quarterly Public Debt (QPD) database. The QPD is exactly what you think it is: a record of sovereign debt managed by the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund (IMF). First, to our `wdi` dataset. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # identify the relevant series families prefixes <- c("NY", "FD", "FB", "IQ", "BN") # subset `wdi` and create `macro_wdi` macro_wdi <- wdi %>% filter(str_detect(`Series_Code`, str_c("^", prefixes, collapse = "|"))) %>% rename_with(~str_extract(., "\\d{4}"), starts_with("20")) macro_wdi ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 70 × 9 Country Country_Code Series_Name Series_Code `2018` `2019` `2020` 1 India IND Adjusted net nat… NY.ADJ.NNT… 1.72e 3 1.81e 3 1.66e 3 2 India IND CPIA debt policy… IQ.CPA.DEB… NA NA NA 3 India IND CPIA macroeconom… IQ.CPA.MAC… NA NA NA 4 India IND CPIA trade ratin… IQ.CPA.TRA… NA NA NA 5 India IND Current account … BN.CAB.XOK… -6.56e10 -2.98e10 3.27e10 6 Canada CAN Adjusted net nat… NY.ADJ.NNT… 3.76e 4 3.78e 4 3.51e 4 7 Canada CAN CPIA debt policy… IQ.CPA.DEB… NA NA NA 8 Canada CAN CPIA macroeconom… IQ.CPA.MAC… NA NA NA 9 Canada CAN CPIA trade ratin… IQ.CPA.TRA… NA NA NA 10 Canada CAN Current account … BN.CAB.XOK… -4.12e10 -3.40e10 -3.54e10 # ℹ 60 more rows # ℹ 2 more variables: `2021` , `2022` ``` ::: ::: Again, take note of the missing values! It's sad that we're missing the CPIA rating variables (starting with `IQ`) for all the countries (Canada, India, Mexico, South Africa and Indonesia). Let's drop the CPIA rows. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} macro_wdi <- macro_wdi %>% filter(!(Series_Code %in% c('IQ.CPA.FINS.XQ', 'IQ.CPA.FISP.XQ', 'IQ.CPA.MACR.XQ', 'IQ.CPA.PROP.XQ', 'IQ.CPA.PROT.XQ', 'IQ.CPA.DEBT.XQ', 'IQ.CPA.TRAD.XQ'))) c(macro_wdi$Series_Code %>% unique(), macro_wdi$Series_Name %>% unique()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "NY.ADJ.NNTY.PC.CD" [2] "BN.CAB.XOKA.CD" [3] "Adjusted net national income per capita (current US$)" [4] "Current account balance (BoP, current US$)" ``` ::: ::: So these are the variables we'll include from the WDI data frame! Now, let's load the QPD dataset. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} file_path_2 <- "datasets/qpd.csv" qpd <- read_csv(file_path_2) %>% rename(Series_Code = "Series Code", Series_Name = "Series Name", Country = "Country Name", Country_Code = "Country Code") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Rows: 623 Columns: 24 ── Column specification ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────── Delimiter: "," chr (4): Country Name, Country Code, Series Name, Series Code dbl (20): 2018Q1 [YR2018Q1], 2018Q2 [YR2018Q2], 2018Q3 [YR2018Q3], 2018Q4 [Y... ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data. ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message. ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} head(qpd, 25) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 25 × 24 Country Country_Code Series_Name Series_Code `2018Q1 [YR2018Q1]` 1 Albania ALB Gross PSD, Total, Sho… DP.DOD.DSO… 2060492. 2 Albania ALB Gross PSD, Total, Sho… DP.DOD.DSL… 0 3 Albania ALB Gross PSD, Total, Sho… DP.DOD.DSI… NA 4 Albania ALB Gross PSD, Total, Sho… DP.DOD.DSD… 1326195107. 5 Albania ALB Gross PSD, Total, Sho… DP.DOD.DSC… 3979442411. 6 Albania ALB Gross PSD, Total, Sho… DP.DOD.DST… 5307698010. 7 Argentina ARG Gross PSD, Total, Sho… DP.DOD.DSO… NA 8 Argentina ARG Gross PSD, Total, Sho… DP.DOD.DSL… NA 9 Argentina ARG Gross PSD, Total, Sho… DP.DOD.DSI… NA 10 Argentina ARG Gross PSD, Total, Sho… DP.DOD.DSD… NA # ℹ 15 more rows # ℹ 19 more variables: `2018Q2 [YR2018Q2]` , `2018Q3 [YR2018Q3]` , # `2018Q4 [YR2018Q4]` , `2019Q1 [YR2019Q1]` , # `2019Q2 [YR2019Q2]` , `2019Q3 [YR2019Q3]` , # `2019Q4 [YR2019Q4]` , `2020Q1 [YR2020Q1]` , # `2020Q2 [YR2020Q2]` , `2020Q3 [YR2020Q3]` , # `2020Q4 [YR2020Q4]` , `2021Q1 [YR2021Q1]` , … ``` ::: ::: The series data in QPD is stored on a quarter-by-year basis. We can aggregate the data *column-wise* to get yearly amounts. > **Note**: R usually throws an error if you're telling it to sum over certain rows/columns that include NA values. We resolve this by setting the parameter `na.rm = TRUE`, which literally means "NA remove is TRUE". Before we aggregate the data, let's check the number of periods for which data is missing. Again, we'll look at the country-series combinations. We do that below with a loop, telling R to *manually* go over each unique row, count the number of NAs along the period columns, and then store the result in another data frame called `status`. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} status <- data.frame() # empty data frame that is placeholder for the final data Series_Codes <- qpd$Series_Code %>% unique() # gets all `Series_Codes` to iterate over Countries <- qpd$Country_Code %>% unique() # gets all `Country_Codes` to iterate over for (country_code in Countries) { select <- filter(qpd, Country_Code == country_code) # first filter for the indexed country with `country_code` for (series_code in Series_Codes) { select_further <- filter(select, Series_Code == series_code) # then filter by for the indexed series with `series_code` cols_to_check <- select(select_further, c("2018Q1 [YR2018Q1]", "2018Q2 [YR2018Q2]", "2018Q3 [YR2018Q3]", "2018Q4 [YR2018Q4]", # then select the period columns "2019Q1 [YR2019Q1]", "2019Q2 [YR2019Q2]", "2019Q3 [YR2019Q3]", "2019Q4 [YR2019Q4]", "2020Q1 [YR2020Q1]", "2020Q2 [YR2020Q2]", "2020Q3 [YR2020Q3]", "2020Q4 [YR2020Q4]", "2021Q1 [YR2021Q1]", "2021Q2 [YR2021Q2]", "2021Q3 [YR2021Q3]", "2021Q4 [YR2021Q4]", "2022Q1 [YR2022Q1]", "2022Q2 [YR2022Q2]", "2022Q3 [YR2022Q3]", "2022Q4 [YR2022Q4]")) # the result will be a single row of period columns for each unique `Country_Code`, `Series_Code` combination na_count <- sum(is.na(cols_to_check)) # finally, store the value of NAs result <- data.frame(Country_Code = country_code, Series_Code = series_code, na_count = na_count) status <- rbind(status, result) # appends the result to the status data frame and iterate over } } head(status) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Country_Code Series_Code na_count 1 ALB DP.DOD.DSOA.CR.PS.CD 0 2 ALB DP.DOD.DSLO.CR.PS.CD 17 3 ALB DP.DOD.DSIN.CR.PS.CD 20 4 ALB DP.DOD.DSDS.CR.PS.CD 0 5 ALB DP.DOD.DSCD.CR.PS.CD 0 6 ALB DP.DOD.DSTC.CR.PS.CD 0 ``` ::: ::: As expected, `status` has three columns: `Country_Code`, `Series_Code`, and the `na_count`. Now let's check which combinations have data missing for less than 20 periods. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} status_to_drop <- status %>% filter(na_count < 20 & na_count > 0) # strictly less than 20 data is missing for *all* of the 20 columns, the aggregate function will take care of the missing values and return `0` as the yearly aggregate value. However, if data is missing for strictly less than 20 period columns, the yearly aggregate values will be under-estimated. These are the countries-series pairs which we must drop from the data-frame. > **Note**: by storing our exploration's results in `status`, we can revisit our decision to drop values anytime we want. Such proper documentation builds trust around the validity of the aggregate computations!
